account: The requested definitions are all present in dung-1995-argumentation.txt with clear page markers. The characteristic function F_AF is defined on page 8 (marker ===== PDF PAGE 8 =====) as F_AF(S) = {A | A is acceptable with respect to S}. The grounded (skeptical) extension is defined on page 9 (===== PDF PAGE 9 =====) as the least fixed point of F_AF, labeled GE_AF. The preferred (credulous) extension is defined on page 7 (===== PDF PAGE 7 =====) as a maximal admissible set under set inclusion. The stable extension is defined on page 8 (===== PDF PAGE 8 =====) as a conflict-free set that attacks every argument not in it. Links to nonmonotonic reasoning and logic programming appear on pages 8, 19-24, and 28-29: page 8 links stable extensions to stable models, Reiter extensions, and autoepistemic stable expansions; pages 19-21 show Reiter's default logic as argumentation with R-extensions corresponding to stable extensions; pages 23-24 show logic programming as argumentation with stable models corresponding to stable extensions and well-founded models to grounded extensions; pages 28-29 give a general method for argumentation-as-logic-programming. Page 18 provides the 'no bug if no stable semantics' result, and page 8 notes that stable semantics is not defined for every framework. The source text is fully available, so sufficiency is ready_to_synthesize.

citations.excerpt: Definition 16. The characteristic function denoted by F_AF of an argumentation framework AF = (AR, attacks) is defined as follows: F_AF(S) = {A | A is acceptable with respect to S}.

claims.statement: The characteristic function F_AF of an argumentation framework AF = (AR, attacks) is defined as F_AF(S) = {A | A is acceptable with respect to S}.

citations.excerpt: Definition 20. The grounded extension of an argumentation framework AF, denoted by GE_AF, is the least fixed point of F_AF.

claims.statement: The grounded (skeptical) extension GE_AF of an argumentation framework AF is the least fixed point of the characteristic function F_AF.

citations.excerpt: Definition 7. A preferred extension of an argumentation framework AF is a maximal (with respect to set inclusion) admissible set of AF.

claims.statement: A preferred (credulous) extension of an argumentation framework AF is a maximal (with respect to set inclusion) admissible set of AF.

citations.excerpt: Definition 13. A conflict-free set of arguments S is called a stable extension iff S attacks each argument which does not belong to S.

claims.statement: A stable extension of an argumentation framework AF is a conflict-free set of arguments that attacks each argument which does not belong to the set.

citations.excerpt: It will turn out later (Section 4) that this proposition underlines exactly the way the notions of stable models in logic programming, extensions in Reiter's default logic, and stable expansion in Moore's autoepistemic logic are defined.
citations.locator: papers/text/dung-1995-argumentation.txt, ===== PDF PAGE 8 =====, text following Lemma 14

claims.statement: Dung states that the notions of stable models in logic programming, extensions in Reiter's default logic, and stable expansions in Moore's autoepistemic logic are defined in exactly the same way as stable extensions in argumentation frameworks.

citations.excerpt: A default theory T = (D, W) can be interpreted as an argumentation framework AF(T) = (AR, attacks); Theorem 43: Let E be an R-extension of T and E' be a stable extension of AF(T), then arg(E) is a stable extension and flat(E') is an R-extension.

claims.statement: Dung shows that Reiter's default logic can be interpreted as an argumentation framework, and that the R-extensions of a default theory correspond exactly to the stable extensions of the corresponding argumentation framework.

citations.excerpt: Theorem 49: A Herbrand interpretation M is a stable model of P iff there is a stable extension E of AF(P) such that M = ... Theorem 50: The well-founded model of P coincides with the grounded extension of AF(P).

claims.statement: Dung shows that logic programming with negation as failure can be viewed as argumentation, with stable models of a logic program corresponding to stable extensions and the well-founded model corresponding to the grounded extension of the corresponding argumentation framework.

citations.excerpt: Stable extensions do not capture the intuitive semantics of every meaningful argumentation system. ... Let P be a knowledge base represented either as a logic program, or as a nonmonotonic theory, or as an argumentation framework. Then there is not necessarily a 'bug' in P if P has no stable semantics.
